Andrew Carnegie

Industry & Giving · Scotland / United States · 1835–1919

2 min read1 figure, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 21 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersWhere it is contestedCorrectedThe definitive biographyReads across to

A bobbin boy at thirteen, the world's richest man at sixty-five, and author of the sentence that indicts every fortune including his own: the man who dies rich dies disgraced.

If you keep one line

Watch the costs and the profits take care of themselves. Then remember Homestead before you admire.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

The Dunfermline weaver's son arrived in Pittsburgh at twelve, worked a cotton mill at thirteen, taught himself telegraphy, and rode the Pennsylvania Railroad's management ladder into capital. Steel made the fortune: he bet early and totally on the Bessemer process, built the Edgar Thomson works, and ran on one commandment — watch the costs, and the profits will take care of themselves. In 1901 he sold Carnegie Steel to J.P. Morgan's syndicate for $480 million, and Morgan made it the core of U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar corporation.

Homestead, 1892, is the permanent stain: a lockout at his own mill, Pinkertons and strikers dead, the union broken for a generation — while Carnegie, philosopher of labour's dignity in print, kept to Scotland and let Frick swing the club. No account of the giving survives without this chapter, and the serious biographies no longer try.

The giving itself was doctrine before it was charity. 'The Gospel of Wealth' (1889) argued the rich are trustees obligated to die poor, having administered their surplus for the community — and he nearly did: some 2,500 libraries, Carnegie Hall, the Peace Palace at The Hague, universities and pensions for teachers, most of the fortune gone before the end. The libraries were the perfect Carnegie instrument: infrastructure for self-improvement, offered to every town that would tax itself to stock and staff one.

02Where it is contested

How much Carnegie knew and directed at Homestead is still argued — his defenders blame Frick, the correspondence implicates them both. And the Gospel of Wealth reads either as the founding charter of modern philanthropy or as capitalism's most elegant apology for itself; a century of argument has not chosen.

03Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 9 · Sept 2026 · Six lives said more than their sources.

A sourcing pass opened the documents behind the figures in eight lives, and six said more than those documents do. Fritz Haber said roughly half the nitrogen in your body came through his process and that three to four billion people are alive because of it. The first line was found in no document opened. The study most often cited gives 48 per cent of the world's population in 2008, and the entry now says that. John D. Rockefeller put Standard Oil's ninety per cent of American refining in the early 1880s; the source opened puts it at 1879. Andrew Carnegie called the 1901 sale the largest transaction in industrial history; neither source opened says so, and the sentence now says what they do. Robert Moses gave thirteen bridges and hundreds of playgrounds as Caro's count; only the $27 billion was found. Steve Jobs said he paid Lucasfilm for its graphics group; by Alvy Ray Smith's account the new company paid for the technology out of Jobs's ten million. Tu Youyou's sixty laboratories are sixty institutions in the WHO's count. Each figure now carries the document it was read in.

04The definitive biography

Andrew CarnegieDavid Nasaw · 2006

The full modern life: unsparing on Homestead, alert to the self-mythologising, and still able to take the Gospel of Wealth seriously as ideas. Replaces the older admiring standards.
